PreProject_Veg_Desc:
Elevations of the fire range from 5,120 feet at the base of Eighteen Mile canyon to
7,848 feet at the top of Delano Peak. Two roads access the fire one is the School
House Canyon road and the Eighteen Mile Canyon Road. Both canyons are narrow
with steep side slopes. In addition, both canyons had pinyon/juniper stands that
were burned in the fire. Soils in the burn area are primarily Shallow Calcareous
Loam 8-10" and Shallow Clay Loam 10-14". There is a small portion of a loamy 8-
10 range site at the base of Eighteen Mile Creek next to the lek. Due to the
topography and location of the two roads there is potential for flash flooding until
the existing vegetation recovers naturally or through seeding treatments in
those areas of the pinyon juniper
The lower and mid elevations that were not within the pinyon and juniper sites
were primarily black sage stands that had a good understory of bluebunch and
Sandberg’s bluegrass. Cheatgrass was present in the burn area and was most
noticeable in the drainage bottoms but was present on some of the unburned side
slopes as well. Fire intensities were high enough to consume the grasses and forbs
and kill the sagebrush and juniper. There were a number of small unburned islands
of juniper noted through parts of the School House portion of the fire. The higher
elevation portions of the fire with the exception of the steep side slopes supported
stands of serviceberry, snowberry, big sagebrush and bitterbrush.
Bluebunch wheatgrass was the dominate grass observed in the higher elevation
areas. Cheatgrass was present in areas adjacent to the roads and has the potential to
increase after the fire in the areas that had moderate burn severity and in the pinyon
juniper stands that burned.
Justification_Desc:
The Delano Fire was a lightning caused fire that burned approximately 15,264
acres, 11,324 acres public and 3,940 acres private. The fire is located about 20
miles north of Montello, NV and about 2 miles south of the 2017 Dry Gulch Fire
on Delano Mountain. The fire burned within portions of previous fire perimeters,
including Division, No School, 21 Mile and Schoolhouse.
The Delano Fire burned primarily within PHMA (49%), and non-habitat (44%). A
total of 5,651 acres is within Sage-Grouse Focal Area (SFA). There is one active
lek (name: “Eighteen mile lek”) within a half mile of the southeastern fire
perimeter. The Delano Fire affected multiple species of big game. Mule Deer,
antelope, and elk all reside within the area and use habitat that falls within the fire
perimeter. The fire affected a total of 11,837 acres of the North Gamble mule deer
herd. The entire burn area falls within pronghorn summer habitat. A total of 11,991
acres of crucial elk habitat were affected, as well as 4,470 acres of crucial summer
habitat.
Criteria_for_Graze: The objective of this activity is to allow for new seedling establishment\r\nand to allow for the natural recovery of native vegetation affected by the burn\r\nthrough adequate grazing rest.

Soil_Desc:
Soils on the site are largely
characterized by loamy soils. The ecological sites within the fire include Loamy 8-
10”, Loamy Slope 12-16”, Shallow Calcareous Loam 8-10” and Shallow Clay
Loam 8-10.” Loamy 8-10” and Loamy Slope 12-16” are the predominant
ecological sites and represent 78% of the burned area.
PreProject_Veg_Desc:
Elevations on the fire range from 5,300 feet to 7,300 feet with an average elevation
of around 6,000 feet. Topography is comprised of a rolling plateau to the northwest
that gradually transitions to a complex range of mountains with Bald Mountain to
the east and Delano Mountain to the south. Soils on the site are largely
characterized by loamy soils. The ecological sites within the fire include Loamy 8-
10”, Loamy Slope 12-16”, Shallow Calcareous Loam 8-10” and Shallow Clay
Loam 8-10.” Loamy 8-10” and Loamy Slope 12-16” are the predominant
ecological sites and represent 78% of the burned area.
Although cheatgrass was common pre-fire, monocultures were uncommon, and
most plant communities contained a perennial herbaceous component. Some plant
communities in the fire were previously unburned. These communities were
largely in the Current Potential State with a sagebrush overstory and a viable
perennial herbaceous understory or were in the Tree State – all woodland phases
were represented. The fire also impacted numerous successful ESR seedings
Justification_Desc:
The Dry Gulch fire was a lightning caused fire that burned approximately 55,328
acres across private (182 acres) and BLM administered (54,146 acres) with low to
high fire severity. The fire is located about 25 miles southeast of Jackpot, NV, and
the southern end of the fire is about 10 miles north of Crittenden Reservoir. The
fire burned within portions of previous fire perimeters, including the 2006 Mustang
and Teepee fires, the 2007 West Fork fire and the 2011 Signboard fire.
The entirety of the Dry Gulch Fire is within a Sage-grouse Focal Area (SFA);
almost 100% of the fire is designated Priority Habitat Management Area (PHMA).
There is one active lek, Signboard Pass, within the fire perimeter. Based on
seasonal habitat delineation conducted by the Nevada Department of Wildlife, the
Dry Gulch Fire contains lek, nesting, early and late brood rearing, and winter
habitats. In addition, the Dry Gulch fire area negatively impacted limited use mule
deer habitat (54,275 acres), elk crucial winter (32,984 acres), crucial summer
(5,992 acres) and winter range (7,191 acres), and pronghorn summer range habitat
(52,006 acres), as well as raptor nesting locations. Habitat burned in the Dry Gulch
fire is very important to the elk population found in the Goose Creek area. In
addition, the Dry Gulch Fire burned 195 acres of occupied habitat for the BLM
Sensitive plant Goose Creek Milkvetch (Astragalus anserinus). This rare, endemic
plant is currently known to occur in the Goose Creek drainage in Cassia County,
Idaho, Elko County, Nevada, and Box Elder County, Utah. Goose Creek milkvetch
(GCM) has been a candidate species for listing under the Endangered Species Act.

Fire intensities were high enough to consume the grasses and forbs and kill
sagebrush. Many wildlife species depend on sagebrush and forbs for cover and
forage and will be severely impacted if these species are not reestablished back
into the ecosystem.
Criteria_for_Graze:
The objective of this activity is to allow for new seedling establishment
and to allow for the natural recovery of native vegetation affected by the burn
through adequate grazing rest.

2018 - Monitoring implementation/effectiveness:
Livestock compliance monitoring will be conducted by ESR and
Range Management staff for the Little Goose Creek, Bluff Creek,
Gamble Individual and Dairy Valley allotments. Grazing closure
monitoring will be conducted along with other treatment
effectiveness monitoring. Additional monitoring of grazing closures
may be needed if trespass livestock are detected within the closure
area.

Drill Bitterbrush Treatment Recommendations 2020:
Monitoring results in the treatment area have shown that rehabilitation objectives have not been fully met in the third growing season. More seeded grass observations were made this year. There was an allotment closure issued for the Gamble Individual allotment, Granite Creek pasture where Plots 01A and 01B are located. The allotment closure objective of three perennial species per square meter was met but it is advised that the area receives appropriate grazing management so that seeded forb and shrub species may establish, especially the antelope bitterbrush which is at risk in the area of not recovering and providing valuable forage to wildlife.

Soil_Desc:
Martin Fire East Soils:
Soils in the Martin Fire area feature an aridic to xeric moisture regime, with annual precipitation
of 8 to 10 inches per year. The elevation of the burn area ranges from 4800 to 6000 ft., with
slopes typically being 30 percent or less. As stated above, most of the fire area is in ecological
site R025XY019NV, a loamy 8-10 P.Z. site. Gravel and stones are common in the soil profile,
taking up plant root space but also offering soil stability and inhibiting erosion. Soil water
holding capacity is low to moderate, and can vary considerably. Soils are a good mix of clay,
sand, and silt (mostly silt and clay) and exhibit vertic properties in the summer when hot and dry.
PreProject_Veg_Desc:
Martin Fire East Background:
Vegetation
Most (90%) of the area of the Martin Fire fell within Ecological Site R025XY019NV, this
ecological site is characterized by shallow loamy soils in an 8-10” precipitation zone. These sites
are characterized by a plant association of Wyoming big sagebrush, Thurber’s needlegrass,
bluebunch wheatgrass, Sandberg’s bluegrass, Indian paintbrush, globemallow, and phlox. Other
alkaline tolerant shrubs like rubber rabbitbrush, fourwing saltbush, and spiny hopsage can also
be found in the plant community in small isolated patches.
Justification_Desc:
Fire intensities in shrub communities were high enough to consume the grasses and forbs and kill
sagebrush. Many wildlife species, including GRSG, pygmy rabbits, mule deer, elk, and
pronghorn depend on sagebrush and forbs for cover and forage. This area is a stronghold for
many wildlife species that has been increasingly impacted by the loss of hundreds of thousands
of acres of sagebrush to wildfire in adjacent areas in recent decades. These wildlife species will
be severely impacted if sagebrush species are not reestablished back into the ecosystem.

The treatments identified in the Martin Fire East ESR plan incorporate local, state, and federal
knowledge of the burned area. We believe these treatments allow flexibility to the livestock
operators while also focusing on Emergency Stabilization and Rehabilitation of the resources
within the burned area. This plan allows us to incorporate adaptive management strategies to
treat next year if the response of the expected natural recovery is low. This area has a high risk of
conversion to cheatgrass so we want to monitor it to ensure we are proactive if cheatgrass
invasion occurs.
Criteria_for_Graze:
The closure is needed to exclude livestock from the burned area to reduce any additional surface soil disturbance which would lead to accelerated soil erosion. This closure will also remove grazing pressures from seeding treatments or the recovery of surviving native perennial vegetation. This action will also reduce the migration of noxious weeds onto the burned area or the spread of existing weed populations.

East - The BLM is working with the livestock permitees on prioritization
of Owyhee Allotment treatments to facilitate and incorporate livestock grazing due to the large
loss of vegetation over the allotment in the last couple of years. Due to the prioritization of the
treatments, the permittees have agreed to rest the seeded areas once treated to allow for
establishment of species until objectives have been met or determined they can't be met.

West - The following allotments were closed: Portions of William Stock, Little Owyhee, Buttermilk, and Spring Creek. All of Sugarloaf was closed.

Criteria_for_Graze:
A grazing closure order was issued January 22, 2021.  The closure is in effect for all BLM lands that were burned or seeded for a minimum of two years to allow for recovery and seedling establishment.  Supplemental methods have been added to AIM to assess range conditions, and help BLM determine when livestock grazing can resume.

The grazing closure ordered continued through fiscal year 2022. Grazing on private lands within the perimeter of the fire has continued during the BLM closure.

As per the 2015 Grand Junction Field Office RMP, areas that have burned will be rested from livestock grazing to allow for vegetation recovery. The Grand Junction Field Office will continue to monitor resource conditions. Data collected will be used to complete Standards and Guidelines Assessments and Evaluations for Healthy Rangelands (land health assessments). All the grazing allotments within the burned area have previous NEPA to authorize grazing within the allotments.
